key_terms.meaning: X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(−st) dt from t = 0⁻ to ∞ (one-sided); s = σ + jω is a complex frequency
The complex plane with σ on the horizontal axis and jω on the vertical axis, where X(s) is drawn
The set of s values for which the integral ∫|x(t) e^(−st)| dt is finite
Integral starts at 0⁻, so initial conditions at t = 0 enter naturally
x(t) = 0 for t < T; its ROC is the half-plane to the right of the rightmost pole
a·x₁(t) + b·x₂(t) → a·X₁(s) + b·X₂(s); ROC is at least the overlap of the two ROCs
x(t − t₀) → e^(−s t₀)·X(s); the ROC is unchanged
dx/dt → s·X(s) − x(0⁻); each extra derivative brings one more initial-condition term
x(t) * h(t) → X(s)·H(s); convolution in time becomes multiplication in s
x(0⁺) = lim(s→∞) s·X(s), valid when X(s) is proper
lim(t→∞) x(t) = lim(s→0) s·X(s), valid only if all poles of s·X(s) lie in the left half-plane
Writing a proper rational X(s) as a sum of simple terms like A/(s − p) whose inverse transforms are known
A factor (s − p)^k needs k terms: A₁/(s − p) + A₂/(s − p)² + … + A_k/(s − p)^k
Degree of numerator < degree of denominator; if not, divide first and separate the polynomial part
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) with all initial conditions zero
A value of s where H(s) becomes infinite, that is, a root of the denominator
A value of s where H(s) = 0, that is, a root of the numerator
Every pole has Re(p) < 0 and the ROC includes the jω axis
Put s = jω in H(s) when the ROC contains the jω axis; |H(jω)| gives gain, ∠H(jω) gives phase
Inverse Laplace transform of H(s); the chosen ROC decides whether h(t) is causal or anti-causal

takeaways: The Laplace transform turns a differential equation in t into an algebraic equation in s, which is why it is used for circuits and control.
X(s) alone is not the answer: the ROC must be stated, because one X(s) can belong to two different time signals.
A pole on the jω axis means a sustained oscillation; a pole in the right half-plane means a growing signal.
Causality and stability are separate questions; a causal system is stable only if all its poles lie in the left half of the s-plane.
Partial fractions plus a table of standard pairs is the practical way to invert X(s), and the ROC fixes the sign and side of each term.
The initial and final value theorems give x(0⁺) and x(∞) from X(s) without any inversion.
For an LTI system at rest, H(s) = Y(s)/X(s), and multiplying by 1/s gives the step response.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit usually start from the defining integral, fix the ROC, then move to partial fractions or pole positions, and close with a stability or system-response conclusion.

bank.q: Define the Laplace transform. Find X(s) and the ROC for x(t) = e^(−at)u(t) and for x(t) = −e^(−at)u(−t). Explain why the same X(s) gives two different signals.
outline: Write X(s) = ∫ x(t) e^(−st) dt with the limits stated
For e^(−at)u(t): X(s) = 1/(s + a), ROC Re(s) > −a
For −e^(−at)u(−t): same X(s), ROC Re(s) < −a
The integral converges in different half-planes, so the ROC is part of the transform

bank.q: State the time-shift and time-differentiation properties of the Laplace transform and derive the differentiation result from the defining integral.
outline: Time shift: x(t − t₀) → e^(−s t₀)X(s), ROC unchanged
Differentiation: dx/dt → sX(s) − x(0⁻)
Derive by integrating by parts, showing where the initial-condition term appears
Extend to the second derivative: s²X(s) − s·x(0⁻) − x′(0⁻)

bank.q: Explain the initial value theorem and the final value theorem. Give one valid use of each and one case where the final value theorem gives a wrong answer.
outline: x(0⁺) = lim sX(s) as s → ∞
lim x(t) = lim sX(s) as s → 0, provided poles of sX(s) are in the left half-plane
Example: X(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)) gives x(∞) = 1/2
Failure case: X(s) = ω/(s² + ω²) has poles on the jω axis, so the limit does not exist

bank.q: Define transfer function, pole, zero and BIBO stability for a continuous-time LTI system. State the pole condition for stability.
outline: H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) at zero initial conditions
Poles are roots of the denominator, zeros are roots of the numerator
BIBO stable when every pole has Re(p) < 0 and the ROC contains the jω axis
Mention that a pole at s = 0 gives a bounded step but not an absolutely integrable impulse response

bank.q: Find the Laplace transform and the ROC of x(t) = e^(−3t)u(t) − e^(−2t)u(−t).
outline: First term: 1/(s + 3), ROC Re(s) > −3
Second term: −1/(s + 2) with ROC Re(s) < −2
Combined: X(s) = 1/(s + 3) − 1/(s + 2)
ROC is the strip −3 < Re(s) < −2, which is non-empty, so the transform exists

bank.q: Find the inverse Laplace transform of X(s) = (s + 2)/((s + 1)(s + 3)) for the ROC Re(s) > −1, and again for the ROC Re(s) < −3.
outline: Partial fractions: A/(s + 1) + B/(s + 3) with A = 1/2, B = 1/2
ROC Re(s) > −1: x(t) = ½(e^(−t) + e^(−3t))u(t), causal
ROC Re(s) < −3: x(t) = −½(e^(−t) + e^(−3t))u(−t), anti-causal
State that the ROC alone fixes the side of each term

bank.q: Find the inverse Laplace transform of X(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)²) for the ROC Re(s) > −2.
outline: Split as A/s + B/(s + 2) + C/(s + 2)²
Final: x(t) = ¼u(t) − ¼e^(−2t)u(t) − ½t e^(−2t)u(t)

bank.q: Solve dy/dt + 3y(t) = 2u(t) with y(0⁻) = 1 using the one-sided Laplace transform.
outline: Transform: sY(s) − 1 + 3Y(s) = 2/s
Partial fractions give 2/3·(1/s) − 2/3·1/(s + 3) + 1/(s + 3)

bank.q: An LTI system has H(s) = (s + 1)/(s² + 3s + 2) with a causal ROC. Find its impulse response and its step response.
outline: Factor the denominator: (s + 1)(s + 2), so H(s) = 1/(s + 2) for s ≠ −1
Pole-zero cancellation at s = −1 must be mentioned
Step response: Y(s) = 1/(s(s + 2)) = ½(1/s − 1/(s + 2)), so y(t) = ½(1 − e^(−2t))u(t)

bank.q: Using the convolution property, find y(t) = x(t) * h(t) for x(t) = u(t) and h(t) = e^(−2t)u(t). Verify the steady-state value.
outline: Partial fractions: ½(1/s − 1/(s + 2))
As t → ∞, y → ½, which agrees with the final value theorem

bank.q: A series RC low-pass circuit has input v_in(t), output v_C(t), R = 1 kΩ, C = 1 µF. Find H(s), h(t), and the response to a unit step. Give the time constant.
outline: KCL/voltage divider gives H(s) = 1/(1 + sRC) = 1/(s + 1000) with RC = 1 ms
Step response: (1 − e^(−1000t))u(t)
Time constant τ = RC = 1 ms; circuit is stable as its single pole is at s = −1000

bank.q: A system has H(s) = (s + 2)/((s + 1)(s − 1)). List the three possible ROCs, and for each say whether the system is causal and whether it is stable.
outline: Poles at s = −1 and s = +1; three ROCs: Re(s) > 1, −1 < Re(s) < 1, Re(s) < −1
Re(s) > 1: causal but unstable, because of the pole at s = +1
−1 < Re(s) < 1: stable but non-causal
Re(s) < −1: anti-causal and unstable
Conclusion: no ROC makes the system both causal and stable

bank.q: Compare the Fourier transform and the Laplace transform. Explain when the Laplace transform reduces to the Fourier transform and how the ROC separates BIBO stability from ordinary bounded response.
outline: Fourier: X(jω) = ∫ x(t)e^(−jωt)dt, exists only if x(t) is absolutely integrable
Laplace: put s = σ + jω; with σ = 0 the two integrals agree
Laplace exists for signals such as e^(2t)u(t) where Fourier does not, because σ can be chosen
Fourier transform exists exactly when the ROC of X(s) contains the jω axis
A pole on the jω axis gives a bounded but not absolutely integrable signal, so it is not BIBO stable for a system

bank.q: A second-order system has H(s) = ωₙ²/(s² + 2ζωₙs + ωₙ²). Draw the pole locations for ζ > 1, ζ = 1, 0 < ζ < 1 and ζ = 0, and explain how the step response shape and stability follow from the poles.
outline: Poles at s = −ζωₙ ± jωₙ√(1 − ζ²)
ζ > 1: two distinct real left-half poles, overdamped, no overshoot
ζ = 1: double real pole, critically damped; 0 < ζ < 1: complex pair, damped ringing at ω_d = ωₙ√(1 − ζ²)
ζ = 0: poles on the jω axis, sustained oscillation, not BIBO stable
Settling time grows as the real part −ζωₙ moves closer to the origin

bank.q: A first-order system y′(t) + a·y(t) = x(t) is built with a = 0 by mistake. Discuss what happens to the impulse response, the ROC and the stability, and what a practical fix is.
outline: H(s) = 1/s; h(t) = u(t) is not absolutely integrable, so the system is not BIBO stable
ROC is Re(s) > 0 for the causal choice and does not include the jω axis, which has a pole at s = 0
A bounded input such as a step gives an unbounded output that grows with t
Fix: add damping so the pole moves to s = −a with a > 0, and check that the ROC now contains the jω axis

glossary.def: The operation X(s) = ∫ x(t)e^(−st)dt that maps a time signal to a function of the complex variable s.
The set of s values for which the Laplace integral converges; it must be stated with every transform.
The complex plane of s = σ + jω used to plot poles and zeros.
A complex value of s at which X(s) or H(s) becomes infinite.
A complex value of s at which X(s) or H(s) equals zero.
A ratio of two polynomials in s.
A rational function whose numerator degree is smaller than its denominator degree.
The coefficient A in the term A/(s − p); for a simple pole, A = (s − p)X(s) evaluated at s = p.
Rewriting a proper rational X(s) as a sum of simple fractions that match known inverse pairs.
A signal that is zero before some time; its ROC is a half-plane to the right of the rightmost pole.
A signal that is zero after some time; its ROC is a half-plane to the left of the leftmost pole.
A signal nonzero for a long range on both sides; its ROC is a vertical strip between two poles.
A Laplace transform integrated from 0⁻ to ∞, used for solving differential equations with initial conditions.
A system whose impulse response h(t) is zero for t < 0.
A system is stable in this sense when every bounded input produces a bounded output; in the s-domain all poles must lie in the left half-plane.
A system whose natural response decays to zero as t → ∞, which happens when all poles are strictly in the left half-plane.
H(s) = Y(s)/X(s) for an LTI system at rest; it multiplies the input transform to give the output transform.
h(t), the output of an LTI system when the input is a unit impulse δ(t); its Laplace transform is H(s).
The output when the input is u(t); in the s-domain it is H(s)/s.
The part of the output caused by the input alone, with all initial conditions set to zero.
The part of the output caused by initial conditions alone, with the input set to zero.
The result x(0⁺) = lim sX(s) as s → ∞, used to read the starting value without inversion.
The result lim x(t) as t → ∞ = lim sX(s) as s → 0, valid only when the poles of sX(s) are all in the left half-plane.
The denominator of H(s); its roots are the poles, which decide the natural response.
